title: Climate Zones
objective: After this level you can name the main climate zones and say where on Earth each one occurs.
summary: Köppen sorted climates by the plants they grow into five groups: tropical near the Equator, dry deserts about 15 to 30 degrees out, temperate, continental interiors and polar.

cards.headline: The ancient Greeks sorted the world's climates with Level 4's lines.
cards.body: They split the world into five zones: a torrid zone between the tropics, two temperate zones, and two frigid zones beyond the polar circles. Not bad for a first draft.

cards.headline: Köppen's map, drawn by plants
cards.body: The system most used today came from Wladimir Köppen, a German climatologist, in 1900. His clever shortcut was plants. What grows in a place depends on its temperature and rainfall, so Köppen drew his climate borders to match the zones of vegetation. The plants had been mapping climate all along; he just read their map. He sorted the world into five main groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar. Here's where each one lives.

items.label: Tropical
points: Hot, humid and rainy all year

items.label: Dry
points: Very little rain, and moisture evaporates fast
Big hot deserts, like the Sahara, lie about 15 to 30 degrees from the Equator

items.label: Temperate
points: Warm, humid summers, often with thunderstorms

items.label: Continental
points: Inside large landmasses, far from the ocean's moderating influence

items.label: Polar
points: Cold even in summer: the warmest month averages below about 10°C

questions.prompt: What did Köppen use to draw the borders of his climate zones?

options.label: Lines of latitude only
options.rationale: Latitude was the Greek approach; Köppen used plants.

options.label: Ocean currents
options.rationale: He matched his borders to plant life.

questions.explanation: Köppen drew his climate borders to match vegetation zones, because what grows depends on temperature and rainfall.

questions.prompt: Why do continental climates have such cold winters?

options.label: They sit right at the poles
They get more rain than anywhere else
They're far from the ocean's moderating influence
They lie in the rain shadow of the Himalaya
options.rationale: Only a few are; distance from the ocean is the rule.

questions.explanation: Continental climates lie inside big landmasses, far from the ocean that keeps coastal places milder.

questions.prompt: From Level 4: the Greeks' torrid zone lay between which two lines?

options.label: The Equator and the prime meridian
options.rationale: Those two lines cross; they don't make a band.

options.label: The Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
The Equator and the Tropic of Cancer
options.rationale: The torrid zone reached into both hemispheres.

questions.explanation: The torrid zone spanned the tropics, from the Tropic of Cancer (about 23.5° N) to the Tropic of Capricorn (about 23.5° S).
